name: Gravitational Lensing
kick: gravity & light · first principles · mass bends starlight
title: Light bending — the 1.75-arcsecond swerve that made Einstein famous
lede: Gravity, Newton said, pulls on things with mass. But light has no mass — so should a star's gravity ignore a passing light ray? Einstein said no, and gave a specific number: light grazing the Sun should bend by exactly twice what any 'gravity pulls on everything' guess predicts. Here is the idea, the computed number, why it is double, where it breaks, and how bending light became a tool for weighing the invisible universe.

sections.h2: 1 · The problem — does gravity touch light at all?

blocks.html: In Newton's picture, gravity is a force between masses: the Sun pulls the Earth because both have mass. But a beam of starlight has no mass. So a strict Newtonian shrugs — no mass, no pull, light sails straight past the Sun untouched. Yet if you take seriously the older idea that gravity accelerates everything equally (a feather and a hammer fall together), maybe a light ray, too, should get nudged as it skims a heavy star.

The stakes are sharp because the two views give different numbers. So this is not philosophy — it is a measurement waiting to be made: by exactly how much does a star's gravity bend a ray of light passing close by?

sections.h2: 2 · The reframe — mass curves space and time, and light follows the curve

blocks.html: Einstein's answer throws out 'force' entirely. Mass, he said, bends the geometry of space and time around it — the way a heavy ball dents a trampoline. Light always travels the straightest available path; but when the ground it travels over is curved, the straightest path is itself bent. So light doesn't get 'pulled' — it goes perfectly straight through a space that is warped, and to us far away the ray looks deflected. The key twist: a mass warps not just space but time as well, and light responds to both. Getting the number right means adding up both effects.

sections.h2: 3 · Seen on a real run — computing the bend past the Sun

blocks.html: We computed the deflection of a light ray grazing the Sun's edge, straight from three measured quantities — the Sun's mass, the speed of light, and the Sun's radius. Every number here is that computation.

headers: bending angle for a ray grazing the Sun
rows: Newtonian guess (light as a falling pebble)
blocks.caption: An arcsecond is 1/3600 of a degree — the width of a coin seen from about 4 km. Tiny, but the two theories disagree by a clean factor of two.

blocks.html: The discovered fact: general relativity predicts 1.75 arcseconds — exactly twice the Newtonian value of 0.88 — and that is what was measured. The bend is real but minuscule, so it can only be seen when the Sun's overwhelming glare is blocked. During the total eclipse of 1919, Arthur Eddington photographed stars near the darkened Sun and found them shifted by the relativistic amount. The factor of two, not the bending itself, is the fingerprint of Einstein's theory over Newton's.

The clean factor of two is the whole story in miniature. A Newtonian who imagines light as a fast little pebble falling in the Sun's gravity gets a nonzero bend — but only from space being curved. Einstein's mass curves both space and time, and a light ray, being the fastest thing there is, feels the warping of time just as much as the warping of space. The two contributions are equal, so the total is twice the space-only guess. Measuring exactly double is therefore a direct confirmation that gravity bends time, not just space.

sections.h2: 5 · The one real limit — it's a whisper unless the mass is huge or you look far

blocks.html: 1.75 arcseconds is desperately small, and it took a rare total eclipse and careful photography to see it at all. The simple formula also assumes the ray only grazes a compact mass and bends a little; close to a black hole, or through a lumpy galaxy, the bending is large and the tidy 'twice Newton' formula must be replaced by a full curved-spacetime calculation. And you can never see the bend directly — only by comparing where a star appears against where it 'should' be, which demands a clean reference and a still, unblurred sky.

sections.h2: 6 · The surprise — bending light became a way to weigh the invisible

blocks.html: What began as a one-off eclipse test is now an everyday tool. A whole galaxy or cluster bends the light of things behind it into arcs, rings, and multiple images — a gravitational lens. Because the amount of bending depends only on the mass in the way, astronomers read the lensing to weigh galaxies and clusters, including the dark matter that emits no light at all. Lensing has mapped invisible mass across the sky, magnified galaxies from the early universe, and even revealed planets around other stars.
The same idea sits at the heart of the subject: gravity is geometry, and light is the ruler that reveals its shape. Trace a light ray and you are reading the curvature of the universe.

recipe.summary: Compute the deflection of a light ray grazing the Sun's edge from the Sun's mass, the speed of light, and the Sun's radius (the impact parameter). Compare general relativity's 4GM/(c^2 R) to the Newtonian 2GM/(c^2 R). numpy, SI units.
recipe.eq:
Schwarzschild radius r_s = 2GM/c^2 = 2.95 km for the Sun
deflection (general relativity) = 4GM/(c^2 R) = 1.75 arcseconds
deflection (Newtonian pebble)   = 2GM/(c^2 R) = 0.88 arcseconds  (exactly half)
